<description>
While playing around with pruning for the kernel, I noticed that only bitcoind's init locks the blocks directory (`AppInitLockDirectories`). The kernel doesn't.

Pointing a kernel program at a running node's data directory fails, but only because LevelDB locks `blocks/index`. To avoid a second copy of the chain, the obvious workaround is to use the node's blocks directory with the program's own data directory, or in-memory databases. It starts without error, but with an empty block index `BlockManager` writes from offset 0 of the node's `blk00000.dat`, which `FlatFileSeq::Open` opens in place with `"rb+"`. The node keeps running and serves the overwritten bytes as its own blocks.

#31674 added the blocks directory lock to bitcoind and noted that "the kernel does not currently do any dir locking, but it should". This PR follows sedited's [suggestion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31674#pullrequestreview-2560427054) to add the lock to the `BlockManager` constructor, and is based on the [`lock_blocksdir_raii`](https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/commit/e08ecc19b37b23ee936c3b14b75b3852efd1d23c) commit.

`BlockManager` holds `.lock` for its whole lifetime through `BlocksDirLock`, its first member, so the directory is locked before `xor.dat` is touched. Creating a chainstate manager on a blocks directory locked by another process, bitcoind or a kernel user, fails.

In bitcoind, init already holds the lock, so `LockDirectory` returns success without locking again. The lock is released when the `BlockManager` is destroyed rather than at exit. That happens at shutdown, and when a GUI user retries a failed chainstate load with a reindex, after which the new `BlockManager` reacquires it. A blocks directory used through the kernel now has to be writable, as bitcoind already required.

Added a regression test to feature_filelock.py.
</description>
